notes:
Task and constraints: Given n line heights (2 <= n <= 10^5), pick two lines that with the x-axis hold the most water; area is the smaller height times the distance.
Idea: Start with the widest pair at both ends. Record its area, then move inward the pointer at the shorter line, repeating until the pointers meet.
Technique and why it applies: Two pointers. Moving the taller line cannot raise the limiting height while the width shrinks, so only moving the shorter side can improve the area.
Invariant: Every pair that uses a position already passed by a pointer is no better than the best area recorded so far.
Edge cases: Equal heights move the right pointer, which is safe; zeros give area 0; n = 2 evaluates exactly one pair.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each step moves a pointer and they meet after n - 1 steps. Space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Convert an integer from 1 to 3999 to a Roman numeral.
Idea: Keep a table of the 13 values that form numerals, including subtractive ones such as 900 (CM) and 4 (IV). Go through them from largest to smallest and append the symbol while the value still fits into num, subtracting each time.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy. Because the table includes the subtractive pairs, taking the largest value that fits always produces the standard numeral.
Invariant: The string r plus the Roman form of the remaining num always equals the Roman form of the original number.
Edge cases: 4 and 9 at each decade use the subtractive entries; 3999 gives MMMCMXCIX; the loop never runs forever because every pass subtracts a positive value.
Complexity: Time is O(1) because num is at most 3999, so at most 15 symbols are appended (O(log num) in general). Space is O(1) apart from the output.

Task and constraints: Convert a valid Roman numeral of length 1 to 15 into an integer in [1, 3999].
Idea: Look at each symbol and the one after it. If the current value is smaller than the next one, subtract it, otherwise add it. The last symbol is always added.
Technique and why it applies: A single left-to-right scan with one symbol of lookahead captures the subtractive rule (IV, IX, XL and so on).
Invariant: After processing index i, sum equals the value of the prefix s[0..i] with the last symbol not yet added.
Edge cases: A single-character string skips the loop and returns that symbol's value; the variable name sum shadows the built-in, which is harmless here; input is guaranteed valid, so no error handling is needed.
Complexity: Time is O(n) for one pass with dictionary lookups. Space is O(1) because the table has seven fixed entries.

Task and constraints: Roman numeral to integer, length up to 15, input guaranteed valid.
Idea: Add each symbol's value. When a symbol is larger than the previous one, the previous was subtractive and was already added, so add this value minus twice the previous one.
Technique and why it applies: Single pass with one symbol of memory; the correction term -2 * previous undoes the earlier addition and applies the subtraction.
Invariant: decimal always equals the numeric value of s[0..i] after step i.
Edge cases: The i > 0 test protects the first index; IV gives 1 + (5 - 2) = 4; IX, XL, XC, CD and CM follow the same pattern; repeated symbols just add.
Complexity: Time is O(n) with constant-time lookups. Space is O(1) for the fixed dictionary.

Task and constraints: Find the longest common prefix of up to 200 lowercase strings, each up to 200 characters; strings may be empty.
Idea: Use zip(*strs) to get the i-th character of every string as a tuple. While all characters in the tuple are equal, append the character to the prefix; stop at the first tuple that differs.
Technique and why it applies: zip stops at the shortest string, so the loop is bounded by the shortest length without extra checks.
Invariant: prefix is the common prefix of all strings up to the position already examined.
Edge cases: An empty string among the inputs makes zip produce nothing and the result is ""; a single string returns itself; a different first letter returns "" immediately.
Complexity: Time is O(n * k) for n strings and k the length of the common prefix (plus one failing column). Space is O(k) for the prefix built, plus a tuple of n characters at a time.

Task and constraints: Longest common prefix of up to 200 strings, each up to 200 lowercase letters.
Idea: Compare column by column against the first string. For each index i of strs[0], check every other string; at the first string that is too short or has a different character, return strs[0][:i].
Technique and why it applies: Vertical scanning stops at the earliest mismatch, so no work is done past the answer length.
Invariant: When the loop reaches index i, the first i characters of strs[0] are a prefix of every string.
Edge cases: An empty list returns ""; if strs[0] is entirely a prefix of all others the loop ends and strs[0] is returned; an empty first string skips the loop and returns it.
Complexity: Time is O(n * k) in the worst case, with n strings and k the shortest length. Extra space is O(1) besides the returned slice.

Task and constraints: Return all unique triplets of nums that sum to 0; length 3 to 3000, values up to 10^5 in magnitude.
Idea: Sort the array. For each i, search the rest with two pointers l and r for pairs that sum to -nums[i]. After recording a triplet, advance l past equal values. Skip repeated nums[i] values.
Technique and why it applies: Sort plus two pointers reduces the cubic search to quadratic and makes duplicate removal a matter of skipping neighbours.
Invariant: For the current i, all pairs strictly between l and r that could still reach the target lie inside [l, r].
Edge cases: Once nums[i] is positive, no triplet can sum to zero and the loop breaks; arrays of all zeros return one triplet; the function sorts nums in place.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) after an O(n log n) sort. Extra space is O(1) beyond the sort and the output list.

Task and constraints: Unique triplets summing to 0 in an array of 3 to 3000 integers.
Idea: Sort a copy, fix i (skipping a value equal to the previous one), and move j from the left and k from the right. Move j up when the sum is negative, k down when positive; on a hit record the triplet and skip equal values on both sides.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted two-pointer search per fixed element gives quadratic time and removes duplicates by skipping equal neighbours.
Invariant: For fixed i, every valid pair lies within [j, k]; the two skip loops keep recorded triplets distinct.
Edge cases: The loop stops at len - 2 so two elements remain; i == 0 is handled separately from the duplicate test; negatives, zeros and many equal values are all covered by the skips.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2). Extra space is O(1) beyond the sorted copy and the output.

Task and constraints: Unique zero-sum triplets in an array of up to 3000 values.
Idea: Sort, then fix the largest element at index i going from the end. Skip it if it equals the next one up. Use two pointers on the prefix [0, i-1] to find pairs summing to -nums[i], skipping duplicates after every hit.
Technique and why it applies: Fixing the largest element and scanning the prefix is the mirror of the usual smallest-first version, and still needs only a quadratic pointer sweep.
Invariant: All triplets whose largest element is at a position above i have already been collected, and each is recorded once.
Edge cases: The loop starts at index 2 so there are two candidates below; the check i+1 < len(nums) guards the first iteration; the pointer-duplicate skips use left < right to avoid overrun.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) after sorting. Space is O(1) besides the output and the in-place sort.

Task and constraints: Return the sum of three numbers closest to target. n is 3 to 1000 and exactly one answer is assumed.
Idea: Sort. For each i, move l and r inward: l up if the sum is below target, r down otherwise. Track the sum with the smallest distance to target.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted two pointers explore the sums near the target in linear time per i.
Invariant: closet always holds the best sum seen so far over all examined triples.
Edge cases: The code never returns early on an exact match but still ends on it because the distance 0 cannot be beaten; a leftover print(sum3) writes a line per inner step, which slows large inputs and should be removed for production.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) after the sort. Space is O(1) besides the sort.

Task and constraints: Closest three-sum to target, n from 3 to 1000, values within 1000.
Idea: Sort, fix the largest element at i going down, skip repeated values of nums[i], and sweep left and right pointers over the prefix. Return target immediately when a sum matches; otherwise keep the sum with the smallest absolute difference.
Technique and why it applies: Two pointers on a sorted prefix with early exit and duplicate skipping.
Invariant: result and min_diff describe the best triple among all (left, right, i) combinations already visited.
Edge cases: The first iteration check i+1 < len(nums) avoids indexing past the end; an exact hit returns early; with n = 3 the single triple is evaluated.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) after the sort. Space is O(1) besides the in-place sort.

Task and constraints: Return all letter combinations for a digit string of length 0 to 4 over digits 2-9; the empty string gives [].
Idea: Build the answer from the last digit to the first. Start with [""]. For each digit, repeat the current list once per letter, then prefix each copy with its letter.
Technique and why it applies: Iterative Cartesian product by list extension, with no recursion.
Invariant: After processing the digits from the end up to some position, result holds every combination for that suffix of digits.
Edge cases: An empty input returns [] before the loop; digits 7 and 9 have four letters; the repeated extension uses indices modulo the old length to copy.
Complexity: Time is O(n * 4^n) because up to 4^n strings of length n are produced. Space is O(1) beyond the output list, as the labelled complexity states.

Task and constraints: Letter combinations of up to 4 digits from 2 to 9, in any order.
Idea: Depth-first backtracking. At position n, try each letter mapped to digits[n], append it to the current path, recurse to the next digit, then remove it. When the path has one letter per digit, join and record it.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking over a fixed number of levels enumerates the Cartesian product naturally.
Invariant: curr always holds exactly one chosen letter for each of the first n digits.
Edge cases: The empty string returns [] before recursion; the append and pop pair restores the path after each branch; recursion depth is at most 4.
Complexity: Time is O(n * 4^n) since each of up to 4^n leaves is joined into a string of length n. Extra space is O(n) for the path and recursion, excluding the output.

Task and constraints: Letter combinations for at most 4 digits from 2 to 9.
Idea: Compute the total count as the product of letter counts. For each index i from 0 to total - 1, decode it like a mixed-radix number: for each digit, divide a base by that digit's letter count and take (i // base) % count as the letter index.
Technique and why it applies: Mixed-radix counting enumerates all combinations without recursion or intermediate lists.
Invariant: For each i the chosen letters form a unique combination, and the combinations appear in the same order as nested loops would give.
Edge cases: Empty input returns []; the base is reset to total for every i; each digit contributes between 3 and 4 letters, so there is no division by zero.
Complexity: Time is O(n * 4^n) because each of up to 4^n combinations takes n steps to build. Extra space is O(n) per combination besides the output list.

Task and constraints: Return unique quadruplets that sum to target; n up to 200, values up to 10^9 in magnitude.
Idea: Sort. Fix i and j, then use two pointers l and r to find the remaining pair. Record a quadruplet only if it is not already in the result list, and skip equal values of l after moving it.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting plus two pointers cuts the search from four nested loops to three; duplicates are removed by a list-membership check.
Invariant: res contains each distinct quadruplet found so far exactly once.
Edge cases: Fewer than four elements returns []; Python integers do not overflow with 10^9 values; the membership test a not in res is a linear scan that can dominate when many answers exist.
Complexity: Time is O(n^3) pointer steps plus a linear scan of res on each hit, so it is not tightly bounded by O(n^3) when the answer set is large. Space is O(1) apart from res.

Task and constraints: Unique quadruplets with a given sum for up to 200 numbers.
Idea: Index all pairs (i, j) by their sum in a dictionary, avoiding storing pairs that repeat the same first value. Then for every pair (c, d) look up target minus their sum and combine with stored pairs whose second index is below c, deduplicating through a hash of the sorted quadruple string.
Technique and why it applies: A meet-in-the-middle idea over pair sums replaces one nested loop with a hash lookup.
Invariant: Every stored pair (a, b) satisfies a < b, and the check b < c ensures the four indices are distinct and ordered.
Edge cases: Duplicate values are filtered both when pairs are stored and when quadruples are hashed; a missing key in lookup is skipped; hashing " ".join(str(quad)) is only an identity key.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2 * p), where p is the number of stored pairs sharing the same pair sum, as the author labels it. Space is O(n^2 * p) for the pair table.

Task and constraints: Unique quadruplets summing to target for up to 200 numbers.
Idea: Store every index pair (i, j) in a dictionary keyed by the pair sum. For each key, pair its list with the list for target minus the key, require four distinct indices, sort the four values and add the result if it is not already present.
Technique and why it applies: Pair-sum hashing, a meet-in-the-middle approach, which avoids pointer scans but must filter duplicates afterwards.
Invariant: A quadruple is added only if its four indices are distinct, so no element is used twice.
Edge cases: Index comparison uses "is" on small integers, which works for these index values but is fragile; duplicates are detected by a linear quad not in result check; the final sorted(result) fixes the order.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2 * p), which approaches O(n^4) when many pairs share a sum, following the author's label. Space is O(n^2) for the pair table.

Task and constraints: Unique quadruplets that sum to target for up to 200 numbers.
Idea: Sort. Fix i and j with duplicate skipping, set total = target - nums[i] - nums[j], and run two pointers left and right over the rest. On a match record it, move both pointers and skip equal values.
Technique and why it applies: Two nested loops plus a sorted two-pointer scan is the standard k-sum reduction.
Invariant: For fixed i and j, every pair between left and right that could complete the sum is still inside the window.
Edge cases: The skip tests j != i + 1 and i > 0 stop equal first or second elements from repeating; ranges end at len - 3 and len - 2 so at least two elements remain; sums with 10^9 values are safe in Python.
Complexity: Time is O(n^3), two loops with a linear sweep. Extra space is O(1) besides the output and the in-place sort.

Task and constraints: Decide whether a string of up to 10^4 bracket characters is valid.
Idea: Repeatedly delete the adjacent pairs "()", "{}" and "[]". If the string becomes empty it was valid; if no pair can be removed and characters remain, it is not.
Technique and why it applies: A valid sequence collapses to empty when matched neighbours are removed, so repeated reduction decides it.
Invariant: Each removal keeps the validity of the string unchanged, because it removes a correctly matched adjacent pair.
Edge cases: An odd length can never reduce to empty; a string like "([)]" has no adjacent pair left and returns False; "{[]}" collapses from the inside out.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) in the worst case, because each pass costs O(n) and up to n/2 passes may be needed. Space is O(n) for the new strings created by replace.

Task and constraints: Check that brackets in a string of up to 10^4 characters are properly matched and nested.
Idea: Push every opening bracket on a stack. For a closing bracket, pop the stack and compare its partner with the current character; a mismatch or an empty stack means invalid. The string is valid only if the stack is empty at the end.
Technique and why it applies: A stack remembers the most recent unclosed bracket, which is exactly the one that must be closed first.
Invariant: The stack holds the opening brackets that are still unmatched, in the order they were opened.
Edge cases: A closing bracket first meets an empty stack and returns False; leftover opening brackets make the final length check fail; the input only contains the six bracket characters.
Complexity: Time is O(n), one pass with constant-time stack operations. Space is O(n) in the worst case when all characters are opening brackets.
